title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
content:
Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
Meta’s new business terms could still help it justify training AI on scraped sites.
Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.
Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

report.summary: Meta dropped explicit AI 'training' language from business terms, but experts say the revised wording may still let it scrape news sites to develop AI.
report.background: Meta’s updated business terms, effective October 30th, initially appeared to let the company use any content from websites linked to business accounts to develop, research, and train its AI products. Legal experts warned that could let Meta argue its commercial terms override robots.txt, the longstanding signal scrapers use to indicate what they may crawl. After publishing-industry backlash, Meta removed the word “train.” But experts told Nieman Lab that remaining language about developing “business products” and using content “associated with” a business account may still permit scraping and AI training. Meta denies the update is about scraping news sites or creating rights that supersede robots.txt preferences.
key_points: Meta’s original business terms said it “may use any content” from websites associated with business accounts to “develop, research” and “train” Meta products. Experts warned this could let Meta argue its commercial terms override robots.txt and other blocking instructions.

After backlash, Meta removed explicit “train” language but kept broad wording about developing “business products.” Attorneys say “develop” can be read broadly enough to include training AI models, leaving the core concern unresolved.

The “associated with your products or services” language still worries experts because it could let Meta justify scraping entire news sites, not just limited pages. Meta says the terms are not about scraping news sites.

Meta maintains that robots.txt remains a valid way for content owners to signal preferences and that the update does not give it new rights superseding those preferences. Critics say contractual ambiguity still matters.
The dispute highlights how robots.txt is a technical signal, not a legal ban. Publishers may need stronger contractual, technical, or regulatory protections against AI crawlers.
report.impact: The fight shows that AI training-data rules are increasingly being fought through terms of service, not just copyright law. For AI companies, ambiguous contract language may offer room to scrape and train, but it also invites litigation and regulatory scrutiny. Developers should treat data provenance and site terms as compliance risks, not afterthoughts. Publishers may tighten access, deploy paywalls or crawler blocks, and push for clearer rules. Regular users could eventually see changes in what news is accessible, how AI summaries cite sources, and whether publishers restrict content to negotiate licensing deals. The immediate effect is uncertainty: Meta’s wording changed, but the legal meaning of robots.txt and business terms remains contested.
report.tools: To follow this, monitor Meta’s business terms and robots.txt policies. Useful tools include robotexclusionrulesparser for Python, Scrapy’s RobotsTxtMiddleware, Common Crawl for public web-data research, and Have I Been Trained? for checking dataset inclusion. Publishers can use robots.txt validators and crawler logs; developers should document data provenance and review site terms before training.
